oben.15: The demo needs JavaScript. But the point can be worked out on paper just as well:
oben.16: 440 minus 432 is eight hertz. Two tones eight hertz apart cancel each other out eight times a second — that pulsing is what you hear, and it is how people have tuned instruments for centuries: you wait until it stops.
oben.17: The Tuner does to your entire system audio what this slider does to two tones.
oben.25: Two sine tones in your browser. What pulses is the beating — two close tones cancelling each other in turn. That is how instruments have been tuned for centuries: you wait until it stops. The Tuner itself shifts the finished sound, without touching the tempo.

beweis.35: There is not a single user yet — so we quote none. What there is: numbers from the build and from measurement. They are here together with why they matter.
beweis.36: 11 ms latency with the fast engine That is the line between “works with video” and “does not”: the sound stays on the lips. If you would rather have quality than sync, switch to the good engine — 240 ms, unusable with picture.
beweis.37: 0 allocations in the real-time path Not claimed, checked: the build script takes the finished library apart and lists every call that leads out of the real-time path. There are none. No memory, no lock — and therefore nothing that can crackle in the middle of a track.
beweis.38: 88 tests, 436 assertions, zero failures Built on macOS 26 with Xcode 26.6. The number is here because it is produced afresh with every build — it is not a badge, it is today's measurement.
beweis.39: 432.33 Hz measured — three systems, one result 440 Hz in, target 432: out come 432.33 Hz with the fast engine and 432.09 Hz with the good one. On macOS, on Linux and on Windows. Deviation between them: 0.01 cents.
beweis.40: 0.09 % of one processor core That is 1077 times real time. The fan does not notice anything is running, and neither does the battery — so there is no reason to switch the Tuner off in between.
beweis.41: 0 requests to third-party servers This page loads nothing: no font from Google, no analytics, no cookie. The Tuner asks for no account, no e-mail address, and sends nothing anywhere. You download a file, and that is that.
beweis.42: A recording at 443.1 Hz — the value common in Germany today — brought to 432.0. Not a screenshot: computed, not photographed.

frage.66: There for whoever asks. Out of the way for whoever wants to download.
frage.68: A concert pitch. It fixes where a′ sits, and everything else follows from that. The standard says 440 Hz; 432 Hz lies eight hertz below it, which is −31.77 cents, just under a third of a semitone.
frage.69: The Tuner shifts the whole sound by exactly that distance. It does not pick out individual notes, and it changes nothing about the music except its pitch.
frage.70: So where does 440 Hz come from?
frage.71: From an agreement, not from nature. In 1885 Alexander J. Ellis collected five hundred years of European tuning pitches; his table ran from 370 to 567 Hz — more than a fifth apart. Organ pipes were built to the local unit of length, and the “foot” in France was not the “foot” in Saxony.
frage.72: 440 was settled at a conference in May 1939. 439 was also on the table — it lost because it is a prime number and could not be produced from the BBC's crystal oscillator by dividing down. Out of that awkwardness came a world standard.
frage.74: Small studies, mixed results, no meta-analysis, no independent replication — undecided. That is the state of it, and we report it in both directions without dressing it up.
frage.75: Aravena et al. (2020) found an advantage for 432 Hz in salivary cortisol before a tooth extraction (0.49 against 1.35 and 1.59 µg/dL); on the anxiety scale there was no difference between 432 and 440. Jebabli et al. (2025) found the opposite, with 440 Hz ahead — but that study measured the anaerobic performance of kickboxers during a warm-up, not listening.
frage.76: That listening to music is relaxing is well established. That it is down to the tuning is not. So we promise you no effect. We give you a slider.
frage.78: No. The IYAMBAE Tuner is not a medical device, not a remedy and not a therapeutic instrument. It is a tool that shifts pitch.
frage.79: It is not intended to detect, treat or alleviate any illness, and we claim that nowhere. If something is wrong with you, see a doctor.
frage.80: What about 528 Hz and the Solfeggio frequencies?
frage.81: 528 Hz is not a concert pitch but a single note — roughly a c″. The Tuner shifts the whole sound by an interval; it does not set an individual note. It can still be worked out: if you want your c″ at 528 Hz, set a′ to 444.0 Hz — the slider goes there.
frage.82: About the Solfeggio frequencies themselves we say nothing. There is no neutral encyclopaedia article on them; what you find comes mostly from people selling something.
frage.84: macOS 14.4 and newer — the full app in the menu bar, driverless. Linux with PipeWire 0.3.60 and newer — tray icon, tunings by name, switching while it runs. Built for Debian 13; Ubuntu and Zorin need a rebuild.
frage.85: Windows has an app with a window, a tray icon and the file tool — but no system audio yet. For that the software would have to become the output device itself; a virtual audio device is the next step.
frage.87: Because that is where the sandbox ends, not where the effort does. On iOS there is no equivalent in any form. On Android you may only capture another app's audio if that app permits it — and Spotify, Netflix and YouTube do not.
frage.88: What would be possible is something else: a player of our own that handles the music itself. It is being considered.
frage.89: Why an app and not simply a website?
frage.90: Because a website has to guess and the app can measure. A page in the browser assumes the recording sits at 440 Hz and applies a fixed factor. With a recording at 443 — the value common in Germany today — that lands you on 435 instead of 432.
frage.91: The Tuner determines the actual tuning of the sound as it plays and works out the distance to the target from that. And then there is access: the browser touches only what runs inside it. The app touches everything.
frage.92: How much latency does it cost?
frage.93: Shifting pitch without touching tempo costs time — and how much depends on the method. You choose.
frage.94: 11 msDelay line. Fast enough for video and for playing along. The sound stays on the lips.
frage.95: 240 msHigh quality (Signalsmith). Sounds better, but is unusable with video — a quarter of a second of offset is visible.
frage.96: The switch crossfades over 25 ms so the change does not click.
frage.97: What has this got to do with the radio?
frage.98: If the Tuner is running on the same computer, IYAMBAE Radio can notice and switch off its own guesswork retuning. Then the app takes over — the one that measures.
frage.99: You are asked twice — the page asks, and the Tuner asks you. Without your consent no website learns that you use it, not even that it is installed.
frage.101: This test build costs nothing. It asks for no account, no e-mail address and no payment details — you download a file, and that is that.
frage.102: Nothing has been decided about a price for a later, finished version. If that changes, it will say so here.
frage.104: This page sets no cookies, measures nothing and loads nothing from third-party servers. Even the fonts are here — a link to a font library in the USA would send your IP address there before you had clicked on anything.
frage.105: The Tuner needs no account and sends nothing anywhere. It processes the audio on your own machine and records it nowhere.
